1. Improve the building envelope

Direct‐acting (or “direct‐acting”) electric radiators convert virtually 100 percent of the electricity they draw into heat at the point of use. In that narrow sense they are fully efficient – there are no boiler losses, no pipework circulation losses and no chimney or flue losses as with combustion-based systems.  

However, when you look at system‐wide efficiency and running costs, there are some important caveats:  
• Operating cost  
  – Electricity is generally more expensive per kWh than district heating, natural gas or heat-pump systems, so your heating bill will usually be higher.  
• Primary energy and carbon footprint  
  – If your electricity comes from fossil-fired power stations, the overall carbon emissions per kWh of heat delivered can be higher than for renewable district heating or a modern heat pump.  
• Load control and flexibility  
  – Direct‐acting radiators respond quickly and independently in each room, which is convenient for spot-heating but may lead to higher

Here are several practical measures you can take to get the most out of direct-acting electric radiators:

1. Fit a Digital Thermostat and Timer  
   • Install a room thermostat or an integrated electronic control so each radiator only runs to the set temperature.  
   • Use built-in or external timers/programmers to switch off or setback the temperature when you’re out or asleep.

2. Zone Heating  
   • Only heat the rooms in use rather than the entire dwelling.  
   • Fit separate controls on each radiator so you can tailor the temperature to activity (for instance, higher in a bathroom, lower in a guest room).  

3. Optimize Set-Point Temperatures  
   • Lower your comfort temperature by 1–2 °C. Each degree saved can reduce electricity use by 5–10 %.  
   • Use “eco” or “frost‐protection” modes when you’re away for extended periods.

4. Improve Room Insulation and Draft-Proofing  
   • Seal gaps around windows and doors, add draught excluders, and ensure insulation in walls/ceilings

Improving the efficiency of domestic hot water (DHW) systems typically involves reducing heat losses, using more efficient heat‐generation technologies, and cutting overall hot‐water demand. Below are several proven strategies:

1. Insulate storage and distribution  
   • Wrap storage tanks with high-quality insulation blankets (minimum 50 mm of foam or fiberglass).  
   • Insulate all hot-water pipes—especially those in unheated spaces—to reduce standby losses.  
   • Add pipe insulation at bends and fittings to avoid weak spots.

2. Optimize water‐heater settings  
   • Lower the thermostat to 55–60 °C. Each 1 °C reduction saves about 2–3 % in energy.  
   • If you keep it higher to avoid legionella, use periodic “heat sterilization” cycles instead of a permanently high setting.  
   • Install a programmable timer or smart controller to heat water only during periods of actual need (e.g. mornings and evenings).

3. Upgrade to high‐efficiency technologies  
   • Heat‐pump water heater

An energy declaration (in Swedish, “energideklaration”) is a legally mandated certificate that describes a building’s current energy performance and offers measures to improve its efficiency. In Sweden, every residential and non-residential building over a certain size must have an energy declaration before it is sold, newly constructed, or extensively renovated.  

Key elements of an energy declaration include:  
• Building identification and basic facts (e.g. building type, year of construction, heated floor area)  
• Total annual energy use, expressed in kWh/m²  
• An energy class rating from A (best) to G (worst), reflecting overall efficiency  
• Recommendations for cost-effective upgrades (insulation, ventilation improvements, heating system optimizations, etc.)  
• Results of any air-leakage (blower-door) tests

Here are the main advantages of installing solar panels on a building:

1. Reduced Energy Costs  
   • Once installed, solar panels generate electricity at very low marginal cost (sunlight is free).  
   • You offset or eliminate a portion of your grid-supplied electricity, lowering monthly utility bills.  
   • With net-metering or feed-in tariffs, surplus power you don’t use can be sold back to the grid.

2. Environmental Benefits  
   • Solar electricity produces no on-site greenhouse gas emissions, cutting your carbon footprint.  
   • By relying less on fossil-fuel generation, you help reduce air pollution and acid rain.  
   • Renewable energy supports national and municipal climate-action goals.

3. Energy Independence and Security  
   • Generation on-site makes you less vulnerable to rising utility rates and grid outages.  
   • Coupled with battery storage, solar systems can deliver power during blackouts.  
   • In areas with weak grid infrastructure, solar can be a reliable

1. Site suitability  
   • Roof orientation and tilt – south‐facing roofs at an angle between 20°–40° will typically capture the most sun.  
   • Shading – nearby trees, chimneys or buildings can reduce output significantly.  
   • Structural condition – your roof (or mounting surface) must be able to carry the weight of panels and racking.

When shopping for a new refrigerator or freezer, look for the following key energy-saving features:

1. Energy rating label  
   • In Europe: aim for the top classes (A +++, A ++, or A +) on the EU energy label.  
   • In North America: look for the ENERGY STAR® seal.  
   A better label rating directly correlates to lower annual energy consumption.

2. Inverter compressor  
   • A variable-speed (inverter) compressor adjusts cooling power to demand rather than running at full speed all the time.  
   • This leads to smoother temperature control and significantly reduced electricity use.

3. Efficient insulation  
   • Thick, high-performance insulation (often vacuum-panel or polyurethane foam) minimizes heat gain.  
   • Better insulation means the compressor runs less often.

4. Frost-free (no-frost) technology  
   • Automatic defrosting prevents ice build-up on coils, which maintains optimal heat exchange.  
   • Manual-defrost models can lose efficiency over time as ice accumulate

In the EV-charging industry it is customary to distinguish “normal” (or AC) charging from “fast” (DC) charging roughly by power level:

• Normal (AC) charging  
  – Slow: up to 3.7 kW (single-phase home outlets)  
  – Semi-fast: 7–22 kW (three-phase wallboxes or public AC chargers)  

• Fast/rapid (DC) charging  
  – Rapid DC: typically 50 kW and up  
  – Ultra-rapid: 150 kW, 350 kW and above  

By that convention the informal “boundary” between normal and fast charging sits at about 22 kW AC. In practice, any charger above 22 kW is often deployed as a DC fast charger—most operators start “fast” charging services in the 50 kW range.

Load balancing for EV charging is an energy‐management strategy that dynamically distributes available electrical power among one or more charging points so that:  

1. You never exceed the capacity of your building’s service connection or local distribution circuit.  
2. Each vehicle receives as much current as possible without overloading the installation.  
3. Peak‐demand charges and grid stresses are minimized.  

Key aspects and benefits  
• Static vs. Dynamic balancing  
  – Static (or fixed) balancing allocates a predefined maximum load to each charger. Once the sum of all chargers’ set limits reaches the building’s supply capacity, no charger will draw more than its fixed share.  
  – Dynamic balancing continuously measures total draw in real time and adjusts each charger’s power up or down depending on how many vehicles are plugged in and overall building consumption.  

• Local vs. Centralized control  
  – Local balancing is handled by the charging station itself or a master

In most building‐ and lighting‐standards (for example SS-EN 12464-1 and Swedish Boverket’s general recommendations), stairwells are treated as “circulation spaces” with the following typical requirements:

• Maintained horizontal illuminance (on the walking surface)  
 – Recommended average: 100 lx  
 – Minimum: 50 lx  

• Uniformity (minimum/average): ≥ 0.4  

• Colour rendering index (CRI): ≥ 80 (to ensure good visibility of edges and contrast)  
• Correlated colour temperature (CCT): 3 000–4 000 K  

In addition, if the stairwell is part of an escape route, the emergency lighting system must ensure at least 1 lx along the centreline of the route in the event of mains failure.

Improving basement lighting is often about combining more-efficient fixtures, better light distribution and smart controls. Here are several strategies you can consider:

1. Upgrade to LED fixtures  
   • Select LEDs with high efficacy (≥100 lm/W) and a Color Rendering Index (CRI) of 80 or above for accurate color perception.  
   • Use a neutral-white color temperature (around 3 500–4 000 K) to avoid a “cold” or overly “warm” cast.  

2. Increase uniformity and coverage  
   • Space fixtures so that there are no dark pockets – for general storage you’ll normally aim for at least 100–150 lux; for workbenches or hobby areas 200 lux or more.  
   • Recessed or surface-mounted panel luminaires (e.g. 600 × 600 mm LED panels) give very even, glare-controlled light.  

3. Add task and accent lighting  
   • Install under-shelf strips near workbenches or utility sinks for focused illumination where you need it most.  
   • Consider adjustable track lights for areas you reconfigure frequently.

In Sweden stairwells are normally treated as “service spaces” (climate category C) in the Building Regulations (BBR). The requirements and common good practice are:

• Minimum design temperature (BBR category C): 12 °C  
• Recommended operating range for comfort and to avoid cold drafts into apartments: 16 °C to 18 °C  

By dimensioning your heating system so that the stairwell never drops below 12 °C—even on the coldest days—you comply with the regulations. In practice most housing providers set the thermostats around 16 °C to 18 °C for a more comfortable environment and to reduce heat loss from adjoining apartments.
